claims.feature: other: how the record is made
claims.claim: Le Guin says she worked out the kinship rules of the planet O by drawing charts with symbols and arrows.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Foreword to The Birthday of the World (2001)
claims.quote: I drew charts, with male and female symbols, and lines
claims.page: paragraph on A Fisherman of the Inland Sea

claims.claim: 'Mountain Ways' opens with an explicit note addressed to readers unfamiliar with the planet before the story starts.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Mountain Ways', excerpted on the author's official site
claims.quote: Note for readers unfamiliar with the planet O

claims.claim: The headnote sets out the four permitted relationships as a labelled list, each pairing given its own named term.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Mountain Ways' headnote, excerpted on the author's official site
claims.quote: The Morning woman and the Evening man (the "Morning marriage")

claims.claim: A Gethenian narrator explains the offworld convention for numbering years before stating her own.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Coming of Age in Karhide', excerpted on the author's official site
claims.quote: They call the year of some portentous event Year One

claims.claim: Two of the handbook's species entries end on a two-word status code.
claims.source: Le Guin, Rocannon's World (1966), opening handbook entry, quoted by Books & Boots
claims.page: prologue quotation, end of Species I-A entry

claims.claim: The handbook addresses its reader with a bare imperative telling him to note a social division.
claims.source: Le Guin, Rocannon's World (1966), opening handbook entry, quoted by Books & Boots
claims.quote: Note horizontal social cleavage into 2 pseudo-races

claims.claim: The survey entry sends the reader to numbered maps in a parenthesis inside the sentence.
claims.source: Le Guin, Rocannon's World (1966), second handbook entry, quoted by Books & Boots

claims.claim: The same entry cross-refers forward within the document rather than repeating the material.
claims.source: Le Guin, Rocannon's World (1966), second handbook entry, quoted by Books & Boots
claims.quote: see description of intelligent species below

claims.claim: The planetary entry gives the length of a year down to the second.
claims.source: Le Guin, Rocannon's World (1966), second handbook entry, quoted by Books & Boots

claims.claim: Le Guin's Foundation describes Tales from Earthsea as concluding with an account of the world's history, people, languages, literature and magic.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin Foundation, Tales from Earthsea book page
claims.quote: an account of Earthsea's history, people, languages, literature, and magic

claims.claim: Le Guin identifies the flat fantasy prose she is attacking as journalistic prose.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)

claims.claim: Le Guin says journalism deliberately suppresses the author's personality and sensibility to give an impression of objectivity.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: the suppression of the author's personality and sensibility is deliberate

claims.claim: Le Guin says the journalistic technique is right for a newspaper but wrong for a novel and dead wrong for a fantasy.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: This technique is right, for a newspaper.

claims.claim: Le Guin states flatly that speech expresses character, whether or not the speaker or author knows it.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)

claims.claim: Le Guin says most epics are in straightforward language, whether prose or verse, retaining the directness of their oral forebears.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: Most epics are in straightforward language, whether prose or verse.
